title: Build a Sentence
lines: Build a Sentence opens the Writing section. You see a short exchange: one person says something, and the reply is given as a set of word chunks in the wrong order. You put the chunks in the correct order to make one natural, grammatical sentence. It is a fast test of English word order.
## What is on the screen
- A line from the first speaker, for example a question from a classmate or a comment from a coworker.
- Below it, the reply with empty slots and a group of 4-7 chunks (single words or short phrases). Some words of the reply may already be in place.
- You drag or tap the chunks into the slots. You can move them again before you go on.
- Sometimes one chunk does not belong. You must leave this extra chunk out.
## Timing and scoring

There are 10 items, and the whole set takes only a few minutes (about 6 minutes in this app's mock). That is roughly 30-35 seconds per item. Each item is right or wrong: the whole sentence must be in the correct order to score. The Writing section as a whole takes about 23 minutes, together with the email and the academic discussion.
## What is being tested
- Question word order: auxiliary before subject ("Have you finished ...?", "Where did she put ...?").
- Embedded (indirect) questions: no inversion after "Do you know", "Can you tell me", "I wonder" ("Do you know where the lab is?", not "where is the lab").
- Tenses and auxiliaries: present perfect, past continuous, future with will and going to, modals.
- Adverbs of frequency and time: before the main verb but after "be" ("She usually takes the bus", "He is always late").
- Relative clauses: "the book that I borrowed", "the student who sits next to me".
- Passive voice: "The results will be posted on Friday."
- Prepositional phrases and set patterns: "interested in", "depends on", "not only ... but also".
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Read the first speaker's line and decide what the reply does: answers a question, accepts, refuses, asks back, gives information.
- Step 2: Look at the chunks and find the anchor: the subject and the main verb. Every sentence is built around them.

- Step 3: Check whether the reply is a statement or a question. A question mark at the end, or a question word in the chunks, tells you it is a question; then the auxiliary probably comes before the subject.
- Step 4: Place the fixed partners together: auxiliary and main verb, preposition and its object, adjective and noun, "not only" with "but also".
- Step 5: Put time and place phrases at the end, usually place before time ("at the library on Monday").
- Step 6: Check for an extra chunk. If one chunk duplicates a function (two auxiliaries, two prepositions) or has the wrong form, leave it out.
- Step 7: Read the whole sentence in your head. It should sound like something a person would say.
## Worked example 1: an embedded question
> Speaker: The printer on this floor is broken again.
> Chunks: is / do you / the nearest / one / know / where
> Reply: Do you know where the nearest one is?

After "Do you know", the question becomes a statement: question word, subject, verb. So "where the nearest one is", not "where is the nearest one". The question mark comes from "Do you know", which keeps normal question order.
## Worked example 2: adverb position and an extra chunk
> Speaker: How do you get to campus?
> Chunks: the early bus / I / take / usually / am / because of my 8 a.m. class
> Reply: I usually take the early bus because of my 8 a.m. class.
"usually" goes before the main verb "take". The chunk "am" is the extra: "I am usually take" is wrong because "take" needs no auxiliary in the simple present. The reason phrase goes at the end.
## Worked example 3: relative clause and passive
> Speaker: Did you hear anything about the scholarship?
> Chunks: the students / who / applied / will be / in May / contacted
> Reply: The students who applied will be contacted in May.

The subject is "the students who applied" (a relative clause right after the noun it describes). The verb is passive, "will be contacted", because the students receive the action. The time phrase goes last.

! If two orders seem possible, choose the more neutral, common one. Time phrases at the very start are possible in English, but in these items the time phrase usually goes at the end unless a chunk with a capital letter shows otherwise.
## Common traps
- Inverting inside an embedded question ("Can you tell me when does the store open?").
- Putting an adverb of frequency after the main verb ("I take usually").
- Separating a phrasal verb or set phrase wrongly ("look the word up" is fine, "look up it" is not; "depends on", not "depends of").
- Using the extra chunk because it seems to add meaning. Every correct sentence uses the right chunks only.
- Forgetting agreement: a singular subject with "has", a plural one with "have".
- Not reading the first speaker's line: the reply must answer it in a natural way.
## How to practise between mocks
- Revise the grammar points above one at a time, then write five sentences of your own for each.
- Take sentences from your reading, write each one on paper, cut it into chunks and rebuild it the next day.
- Practise turning direct questions into indirect ones: "Where is the gym?" becomes "Could you tell me where the gym is?"
- Learn adverb positions with simple models: "I always", "I have never", "She is often".
- Do sets of 10 items against the clock, aiming for about 30 seconds each, then review the grammar point behind every mistake.

title: Complete the Words
lines: Complete the Words is the first task you meet in the Reading section. It looks like a spelling test, but it is really a test of how well you read: to finish a word correctly you must understand the sentence around it, know which word fits the meaning, and choose the right grammatical form.
## What is on the screen
- A short academic paragraph of about 60-95 words on a topic such as biology, history or economics.
- The first sentence is complete. It gives you the topic and the vocabulary field, so read it slowly.
- After that, 10 words are cut in half. You see the beginning of each word and type the missing letters. The rest of the paragraph is whole.
- You type straight into the gaps. You can move between gaps and change an answer before you leave the screen.

Each of the 10 gaps is scored as its own item, right or wrong. A word is only right when it is spelled exactly, so "recieve" or "studys" earns nothing even though the meaning was clear. One paragraph is worth as much as two or three ordinary reading questions, so it repays care.
## Timing

The task sits inside the timed Reading module (about 30 minutes for all of Reading, two stages). There is no separate clock for each paragraph, so you manage time yourself. A good target is about 2 minutes per paragraph: one quick read, one pass to fill the easy gaps, one pass for the hard ones and a final spelling check. Do not spend 4 minutes on a single gap; leave your best guess and move on, because a blank always scores zero.
## What is being tested
- Vocabulary: which word makes sense here, given the topic and the sentence.
- Word form: noun, verb, adjective or adverb, and the right ending (-tion, -ment, -ly, -ive, -al, -ous, -ity).
- Grammar: verb tense and agreement, plural -s, articles, prepositions, comparatives, pronouns.
- Collocation: words that usually go together, such as "play a role", "take place" or "rely on".
- Spelling: double letters, silent letters and endings that change the stem (happy to happily, decide to decision).
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Read the first sentence and the whole paragraph once before typing anything. Ask: what is the topic, and is the paragraph describing, explaining a cause, comparing or telling a sequence?
- Step 2: Fill the gaps you are sure of first. Many are short function words (the, and, with, which) or very common words.

- Step 3: For each harder gap, decide the part of speech from the words around it before you think about meaning. After "the" or an adjective you need a noun; after "will" or "can" you need a base verb; before a noun you probably need an adjective; between a subject and an object you need a verb.
- Step 4: Use the letters you can see. They limit the possible words a lot. "env..." in an ecology paragraph is almost certainly environment or environmental, and the grammar decides which.
- Step 5: Check grammar endings: does the verb agree with its subject (the population grows, the populations grow)? Is the time past or present? Is the noun singular or plural?
- Step 6: Reread the full paragraph with your answers in place. Fix spelling and any word that sounds wrong in the sentence.
## Word-form and grammar clues
- After a/an/the/this/their and before a verb or preposition: a noun. "The ___ of the bridge took four years" needs construction, not construct.
- Before a noun, or after be/seem/become: an adjective. "The results were surpris..." becomes surprising; "the surpris... result" also takes surprising.
- Next to an adjective or a verb, describing how: an adverb, usually -ly. "grew rapid..." becomes rapidly.
- After a modal (can, must, may, will) or "to": a base verb with no ending. "may affe..." becomes affect, not affects or effect.
- After has/have/had or be in the passive: a past participle. "was discov..." becomes discovered.
- After "many", "several", "a number of", "these": a plural noun. After "much", "a great deal of": an uncountable noun.
- Comparison words: "more ___ than" or "-er than"; "the most" plus an adjective. "far larg... than" becomes larger.
- Linking words show the logic: however and although signal a contrast, so the missing word may be the opposite of the earlier idea; because and therefore signal cause and result.
- Subject-verb agreement across a long subject: "The number of species living in the forests decreas..." takes decreases, because the head word is "number", which is singular.
! The visible letters must stay as they are. You only add letters, so check that your full word really starts with the letters shown.
## Worked example 1
> Coral reefs cover a tiny part of the ocean floor, yet they support a remarkable variety of life.
> Many fi___ (1) shelter among the cor___ (2) branches, and so___ (3) species spend their whole lives th___ (4).
> (1) fish: after "many" we need a plural noun. "fish" has the same form in the singular and the plural, so do not add -es here; "fishes" is used only in special scientific contexts.

> (2) coral: after "the" and before the noun "branches" we need a word that describes the branches. The topic sentence gives it to you: "coral" is a noun used like an adjective, as in "the coral branches".
> (3) some: "so___ species" needs a quantifier before a plural noun. "some" fits; "sort" would need "of".
> (4) there: the sentence needs a place adverb that refers back to the reefs. "their" is a possessive and would need a noun after it.
The key reasoning was always the same: look at the word after the gap and the word before it, decide the word class, then let the visible letters choose among the candidates.
## Worked example 2
> In the nineteenth century, railways changed how people thought about time.
> Before trains, each town set its clocks by the sun, so noon came at slight___ (1) different moments in neighboring places.
> As timetables grew more detai___ (2), this varia___ (3) caused confusion, and companies even___ (4) adopted standard time zones.
> (1) slightly: the gap describes the adjective "different", so it must be an adverb. "slight different" is a classic word-form error.
> (2) detailed: after "grew more" we need an adjective, so the noun "detail" is not enough. The -ed form describes the timetables (they contained more details). Note the single l: detail, detailed.
> (3) variation: after "this" and before the verb "caused", we need a noun. "various" is an adjective and "vary" is a verb.
> (4) eventually: the sentence tells a sequence (confusion first, then a decision), and the gap sits between subject and verb, the usual place for an adverb of time.
! Gap 2 shows a common trap: you recognize the word family at once (detail) and type the base form. Always ask which form the sentence needs before you type.
## Common traps
- Typing a word that fits the meaning but is the wrong form: "decide" where "decision" is needed, "importance" where "important" is needed.
- Forgetting plural -s after many, several, both, these, or third-person -s after a singular subject.
- Mixing effect (noun) and affect (verb), their and there, its and it's, lose and loose.
- Spelling changes when adding endings: begin to beginning, study to studies, rely to reliance, true to truly.
- Filling gaps from left to right without reading the end of the paragraph, which often explains the earlier sentences.
- Leaving a gap empty. A guess with the right word class has a real chance; a blank has none.
## How to practise between mocks
- Learn word families, not single words: produce, product, production, productive, productivity. When you meet a new academic word, write its noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms.
- Practise common endings and their spelling rules: -tion and -sion, -ance and -ence, -able and -ible, -ful (one l).

- Read short science and history texts every day (encyclopedia entries and textbook summaries are ideal). Cover the second half of every second word in one paragraph and try to restore it after a day.
- Keep an error list of every word you spelled wrongly in practice and review it before each mock.
- Revise grammar points that the task checks most: subject-verb agreement, past participles, comparatives and countable versus uncountable nouns.
- Use the flashcards in this app: for each word, say its other forms aloud before turning the card.

title: Write for an Academic Discussion
lines: In Write for an Academic Discussion you join an online class discussion. A professor asks a question, two students have already posted their answers, and you write your own contribution. You have 10 minutes and should write at least 100 words. The task tests whether you can state an opinion clearly and support it with relevant reasons and examples in good academic English.
## What is on the screen
- The professor's post: some background on a topic (for example education, technology, the environment, business or city life) and a clear question with two or more possible answers.
- Two student posts, each giving a different position with a short reason. The students have names, for example Priya and Lucas.
- A text box for your answer and a 10-minute timer. There is no spell checker.
## Scoring

Your post is scored from 0 to 5. High scores go to posts that answer the professor's question directly, add to the discussion with a new idea, explain that idea with specific support, and use varied, accurate language. Length alone does not earn points, but a post well below 100 words is rarely developed enough. About 120-150 words is a good target.
## Method in 10 minutes
- Minute 0-2: Read the professor's question carefully, then the two students. Choose your position. Pick the side for which you can think of the best NEW reason, not the side you believe most deeply.
- Minute 2-3: Plan in key words: your position, one new reason, one specific example or explanation, and which student you will mention.
- Minute 3-8: Write using the template below.
- Minute 8-10: Check that your opening answers the question, that your reason is different from the students' reasons, and fix grammar and spelling.
## Reusable template
> 1. Position (1-2 sentences): In my view, ... / I'd argue that ... / I understand why Priya thinks ..., but I believe ...
> 2. Link to a student (1 sentence): Lucas makes a good point about ..., but there is another reason that matters even more.
> 3. New reason (1-2 sentences): The main reason is that ...
> 4. Support (2-4 sentences): an example from daily life, school, a familiar situation, or a clear explanation of a result. For example, ... / This means that ... / As a result, ...
> 5. Conclusion (1 sentence): For this reason, I think ... / That is why ...
The key word is NEW. Repeating Priya's or Lucas's reason in different words adds nothing to the discussion. You may agree with a student, but then add a reason they did not mention.
## Worked example

> Professor Hughes: Many cities are considering making public buses free for everyone, paid for by taxes. Supporters say it would reduce traffic, while critics say the money could be spent better. Should cities make public transportation free? Why or why not?
> Priya: Yes. If buses are free, more people will leave their cars at home, and that means less traffic and cleaner air.
> Lucas: I disagree. The money would be better spent on more buses and routes. Free buses that are slow and crowded won't convince anyone.

> Model post: I agree with Priya that cities should make buses free, but for a different reason: fairness. People with low incomes often depend on public transportation the most, and fares take a much larger share of their budget than they do for wealthier residents. For example, a student or a part-time worker who rides the bus twice a day can spend a significant part of their monthly income just getting to class or work. Free buses would give them more money for food or books and make it easier to accept jobs further away. I understand Lucas's concern about crowded buses, but these goals don't have to compete. A city could introduce free fares gradually while adding routes. Overall, I think free public transportation is a fair investment in the people who need it most.

Why this works: the first sentence states the position and links to Priya; the reason (fairness for low-income riders) is new; the example is specific and believable; the post responds to Lucas's point briefly; it is about 145 words.
## Worked example 2: a short plan
> Question: Should universities require all students to take a course outside their major?
> Student 1 (Chen): Yes, it makes students more well-rounded.
> Student 2 (Sofia): No, students pay a lot and should focus on the skills for their careers.

> Plan: Position: yes. New reason: employers value people who can work with colleagues from other fields. Example: an engineering student who took a psychology course understands users better when designing a product. Link: answer Sofia's career point by showing that the extra course helps careers too.
Notice how the plan turns the opposing student's argument into an opportunity: you show that your side also serves their goal.
## Useful language
- Giving an opinion: In my view, From my perspective, I'm convinced that, I tend to agree with.
- Referring to others: As Priya points out, Lucas raises an interesting point, but; While I see why Chen believes.
- Adding a reason: Another important factor is, What is often overlooked is, Beyond that.
- Giving an example: For instance, Take the case of, A good example is, In my own experience.
- Concluding: For these reasons, Ultimately, That is why I believe.
## Common traps
- Not answering the actual question, or sitting on the fence without a clear position.
- Repeating a student's reason instead of adding a new one.
- General statements without support ("This is very important for society").
- Spending too long on an introduction about the topic. Start with your position.
- Inventing statistics or research. A clear everyday example is safer and more convincing.
- Running out of time before checking for errors.

! If you cannot think of a new reason, use one of these angles: cost, fairness, time, health, long-term effects, effects on a specific group (students, older people, small businesses), or practical problems with the other side's idea.
## How to practise between mocks
- Practise planning only: give yourself 2 minutes to read a prompt and write a position, a new reason and an example. Do five plans for every full post you write.
- Write one full post in 10 minutes several times a week, then check it with the template.
- Build a bank of reasons by topic: education, technology, work, health, environment, cities.
- Reread your posts and mark every sentence that is general; rewrite one of them with a concrete example.

title: Write an Email
lines: In Write an Email you read a short practical situation and write an email that does three specific things. The reader might be a professor, a landlord, a manager, a club leader, a company or a library. You have 7 minutes. The task tests whether you can write clear, polite, well-organized English for a real purpose.
## What is on the screen
- A situation of about 60-100 words: who you are, what has happened and who you are writing to.
- Three bullet points: the three things your email must do, for example explain a problem, ask for something, and suggest a solution.
- A text box for your answer. The reader and subject are given, so you write the body of the email: greeting, paragraphs and sign-off.
- A timer showing your 7 minutes. There is no spell checker.
## Scoring

Each email is scored from 0 to 5. A high score needs all three bullets answered clearly and with details, a tone that suits the reader, good organization, and a range of accurate grammar and vocabulary. Missing a bullet is the fastest way to lose points. Aim for about 100-150 words: long enough to develop each point, short enough to check.
## Method in 7 minutes
- Minute 0-1: Read the situation and the three bullets. Decide who the reader is (formal or friendly) and write two or three key words for each bullet.
- Minute 1-6: Write the email using the template below. Give each bullet its own short paragraph with one or two specific details.
- Minute 6-7: Check. Is every bullet answered? Are names, dates and numbers consistent? Fix verb tenses, articles, plural -s and spelling.
## Reusable template
> Greeting: Dear Professor Novak, / Dear Ms. Patel, / Hi Lucas,
> Opening (1-2 sentences): who you are if needed, and why you are writing. "I'm a second-year student in your Monday seminar, and I'm writing about ..."
> Bullet 1 (2-3 sentences): explain or describe, with a concrete detail (a date, a place, a reason).
> Bullet 2 (2-3 sentences): ask or request politely. "Would it be possible to ...?" "I was wondering whether ..."
> Bullet 3 (2-3 sentences): suggest, offer or give details. "One option might be ..." "I'd be happy to ..."
> Closing (1 sentence): thank the reader and say what happens next. "Thank you for considering this. I look forward to hearing from you."
> Sign-off: Best regards, / Kind regards, / Thanks, + your name
## Tone
- Formal reader (professor, manager, company, landlord): full sentences, polite requests with would and could, no slang. Contractions such as I'm and I'd are fine.
- Friendly reader (classmate, friend, club member): warmer, with phrases like "Hope you're doing well" and "Let me know what you think".
- Complaints: firm but polite. Describe the facts, then the request. Avoid blaming language ("You never fix anything").
## Worked example 1

> Situation: You live in an apartment near the university. For two weeks the heating in your bedroom has not worked properly, and the nights are getting colder. Write to your landlord, Mr. Okafor. In your email: describe the problem; explain how it is affecting you; suggest a time when a repair person could come.
> Dear Mr. Okafor,
> I'm writing about the heating in my apartment, number 4B. For about two weeks, the radiator in my bedroom has only been warm for an hour or so in the morning, and it is completely cold at night.

> This is becoming a real problem now that the temperature is dropping. I have been sleeping in the living room, and it has been hard to study in my room in the evenings, which is where I keep my desk and books.
> Could someone come to look at it this week? I'm at home every weekday after 3 p.m., and I'm also free all day on Saturday. If it is easier, I can leave a key with the building manager.
> Thank you for your help. I look forward to hearing from you.
> Best regards,
> Mateo Silva

Why this works: each bullet has its own paragraph; there are concrete details (number 4B, two weeks, after 3 p.m.); the tone is polite and firm; the request uses "Could someone ...". It is about 140 words.
## Worked example 2 (friendly tone)

> Situation: You are in a hiking club. The club leader, Yuki, has asked members for ideas for next month's trip. Write to Yuki. In your email: suggest a place; explain why it would be good for the group; mention one thing members should prepare.
> Hi Yuki,
> Thanks for asking for ideas! I'd like to suggest the lake trail near Pine Ridge, about an hour from campus by bus.

> I think it would work well for our group because the path is mostly flat, so newer members won't find it too hard, but there's an optional climb to a viewpoint for people who want more of a challenge. There's also a picnic area by the water where we could have lunch together.
> The only thing is that parts of the trail get muddy after rain, so everyone should bring waterproof shoes and a change of socks.
> Let me know what you think. I'm happy to look up the bus times if we decide to go.
> Cheers,
> Aisha
## Common traps
- Answering only two bullets, or answering one bullet with half a sentence.
- Writing general sentences with no detail ("There is a problem and I need help").
- The wrong tone: too casual to a professor, or very stiff to a friend.
- Spending too long on the first paragraph and rushing the third bullet.
- Not leaving one minute to check for small errors.
! Useful polite requests: Would it be possible to ...? Could you please ...? I was wondering if ... I would really appreciate it if ... These score better than "I want you to ...".
## How to practise between mocks
- Write one email a day in 7 minutes using the template, then reread it and underline where each bullet is answered.
- Build a phrase bank for opening, requesting, apologizing, complaining, suggesting and closing.
- Practise both tones: write the same situation once to a professor and once to a friend.
- Check your writing for your personal error list (articles, verb tenses, plural -s) and review it before each mock.

title: Take an Interview
lines: Take an Interview is the second Speaking task. An interviewer, on video or audio, asks you four questions about one topic as part of a scenario, for example a research study about city life or a survey about study habits. You answer each question in 45 seconds, with no preparation time. The questions move from your own experience to your opinions, a comparison and a prediction about the future.
## What is on the screen
- A short description of the scenario and an interviewer.
- Each question is asked aloud, one at a time. The recording starts right after the question, and a timer shows your 45 seconds.
- There is no preparation time and no second chance to answer.
## Scoring

The Speaking section takes about 8 minutes in all. Each interview answer is scored on a 0-5 scale for how well it answers the question, how well the ideas are developed and connected, and how clear and accurate your language is: fluency, pronunciation, grammar and vocabulary. You do not need a perfect accent, but you must be easy to follow, and you must answer the actual question.
## How the four questions usually develop
- Question 1, personal experience: "How do you usually get to your classes or your job?"
- Question 2, preference or opinion: "Do you think it's better to live in the city center or in the suburbs? Why?"
- Question 3, comparison or broader view: "How has transportation in your city changed compared with when you were younger?"
- Question 4, prediction or recommendation: "How do you think people will travel in cities twenty years from now?"
## Answer framework: A-R-E-C
- A, Answer (1 sentence, first 5 seconds): answer the question directly. "I'd say living near the city center is better, at least for students."
- R, Reason (1-2 sentences): the main reason. "The main reason is that you save a lot of time on travel."
- E, Example (2-3 sentences): a specific example from your life or a realistic situation. "For example, when I lived with my aunt outside the city, I spent almost two hours a day on buses ..."
- C, Close (1 sentence): return to your answer or add a second short point. "So for me, the extra rent is worth it."
This shape fits comfortably into 45 seconds at a natural pace (about 90-110 words). If you finish early, add a second reason or a detail to the example; do not stop at 25 seconds.
## Worked example 1 (scenario: a study about city life, question 2)
> Question: Some people prefer to live in a big city, while others prefer a small town. Which do you prefer, and why?

> Answer: I'd definitely choose a big city, mainly because of the opportunities. In a big city there are more universities, more jobs and more chances to meet people from different backgrounds. For example, my cousin moved from our small town to the capital two years ago. She found an internship at a design company within a month, which just wouldn't have been possible at home. She also joined a photography club and made friends from all over the country. Of course, cities are noisy and expensive, but for someone my age, I think the opportunities matter more. So, yes, a big city for me.
About 110 words: direct answer, reason, a specific example, a short concession and a close.
## Worked example 2 (same scenario, question 4)
> Question: How do you think cities will change in the next twenty years?

> Answer: I think cities will become greener and quieter. One reason is that more people are switching to electric cars and bikes, so the streets should be much less noisy. I'd also expect more parks and trees, because cities are getting hotter in summer and trees help cool them down. For instance, in my city they recently turned an old parking lot into a small park, and now families use it every evening. I imagine we'll see a lot more projects like that. Some things might not change, though; traffic will probably still be a problem in the biggest cities.
Prediction questions are easier when you base your prediction on a change you can already see today.
## Useful spoken language
- Starting: I'd say ..., Honestly, ..., For me, ..., It depends, but mostly ...
- Giving a reason: The main reason is that ..., That's because ..., One thing is that ...
- Giving an example: For example, ..., Take my brother, he ..., I remember when ...
- Comparing: Compared with ten years ago, ..., Back then ..., whereas now ...
- Predicting: I expect that ..., I imagine we'll ..., It's likely that ..., Probably ...
- Buying time naturally: That's an interesting question. Let me think ... (use once, briefly)
## Common traps
- A long introduction before the answer. The first sentence should answer the question.
- Answering a different question, for example describing the present when the question asks about the future.
- Lists of reasons with no explanation ("It is cheap, fast and good"). One reason with a real example is stronger.
- Stopping after 20 seconds, or speaking so fast that you are hard to follow.
- Memorized speeches that do not fit the question. Raters notice.
- Long silences. If you lose your idea, use a linking phrase ("Another thing is ...") and continue.
! Use the right tense for each question: past for "How has ... changed?", present for habits, "will" or "going to" for predictions, "would" for hypothetical questions.
## How to practise between mocks
- Every day, answer four questions on one topic (school, work, technology, health, travel, environment) with a 45-second timer and no preparation.
- Record your answers. Check: did the first sentence answer the question? Was there a reason and an example? How many seconds did you use?
- Build a bank of personal stories (a trip, a difficult course, a job, a family member, a hobby) that can serve as examples for many questions.
- Practise fluency with linking words: because, so, for example, also, on the other hand, in the end.
- Work on pronunciation of word endings and stress, especially in words you use often in answers.

title: Listen to an Announcement
lines: In this task one speaker gives an announcement or leaves a voicemail: a professor changing a class, a librarian explaining new rules, a coordinator describing a field trip, an office reminding students about a deadline. Each recording is about 70-130 words, followed by two questions.
## What is on the screen
- During the audio the screen may show a picture of the speaker or the place. No text of the announcement is shown.
- After the audio, two multiple-choice questions appear with four options each.
- You hear it once only. Notes are allowed.
## Timing
Listening lasts about 29 minutes in total, in two adaptive stages. Each announcement takes about 30-60 seconds to hear, then you answer quickly. Do not wait for a replay; there is none.
## What is being tested
- The purpose: why the announcement is being made (a change, a reminder, a warning, an invitation, new rules).
- Important details: new times, places, requirements, what to bring.
- What listeners must do, and by when.
- Sometimes an inference: who the announcement is for, or what will happen if listeners do nothing.
## How announcements are organized
Most announcements follow the same plan, which makes note-taking easy:
- Opening: who is speaking and to whom ("Good morning, everyone in Biology 101", "Hi Lucas, this is Olga from the housing office").
- Purpose: the main news, usually in the first or second sentence ("I'm calling because", "I want to let you know that", "Please note that").
- Details: what is changing, where, when, and why.
- Action: what listeners must do ("Please make sure", "You'll need to", "Remember to", "If you can't ..., then ...").
- Closing: thanks, contact information, or a reminder of the most important point.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Catch the speaker and the audience in the first seconds. This tells you the setting.
- Step 2: Write the main news in two or three words as soon as you hear it. This answers the purpose question.
- Step 3: Note details in a simple list: time, place, item, deadline. Write numbers carefully, and note any change ("was Rm 3, now Rm 12").
- Step 4: Listen for action language: must, need to, please, be sure to, don't forget, no later than.
- Step 5: Pay attention to the end. Speakers often repeat the key instruction there.
- Step 6: Answer from your notes. For purpose questions, choose the option that covers the main news, not a single detail.
## Worked example 1

> You hear (a professor): Good afternoon, everyone. Just a quick note before you leave. Next Wednesday's lab session won't take place in the usual lab, because the room is being repainted. Instead, we'll meet at the campus greenhouse behind the science building. We'll be measuring plant growth, so please wear closed shoes and bring the data sheet I'll post online tonight. Print it out, because there's no wifi in the greenhouse. If you have a class right before ours, don't worry about being a few minutes late; the walk takes about ten minutes.
> Question 1: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
> A. To explain how to measure plant growth
> B. To tell students about a change of location for a lab session
> C. To ask students to help repaint the lab
> D. To give directions to the science building
B states the main news. A is the activity, a detail. C misuses "repainted". D confuses the science building with the greenhouse, which is behind it.
> Question 2: What does the professor ask students to do?
> A. Download the data sheet in the greenhouse
> B. Arrive ten minutes early
> C. Bring a printed copy of a document
> D. Skip their class before the lab
C, from "Print it out". A is impossible because there is no wifi. B twists "the walk takes about ten minutes". D reverses his reassurance: they may be late, not skip a class.
## Worked example 2

> You hear (a voicemail): Hi Hamza, this is Priya from the Career Center. You signed up for a resume review this Friday at two. Unfortunately, the adviser you were booked with is away at a conference that day. We can move you to Monday at the same time with a different adviser, or you can keep Friday and do the session online with another colleague. Please call us back or reply to the confirmation email by Thursday noon so we can hold your place. Thanks!
> Question: What must Hamza do?
> A. Attend a conference on Friday
> B. Choose one of two options before a deadline
> C. Send his resume to the adviser by Monday
> D. Call the adviser who is away
B summarizes the request: pick Monday or online Friday, and reply by Thursday noon. A uses "conference" from the reason; C and D are not asked.
## Common traps
- A detail dressed as the purpose: the activity, the reason, or the location of something else.
- Reversed or mixed details: old room versus new room, the reason for a change versus the change.
- Numbers and times: the original time versus the new time, a duration versus a clock time.
- Words from the recording used with a different meaning or a different person.
! When you hear "instead", "now", "moved to" or "no longer", write the new information and cross out the old. Questions very often test the change.
## How to practise between mocks
- Listen to real announcements: university welcome videos, airport and station announcements, museum audio guides, recorded phone messages.
- After each one, write a three-line summary: purpose, key details, action required.
- Practise writing numbers, times and days quickly while listening; this is where many points are lost.
- Learn the language of instructions and requirements: mandatory, optional, required, in advance, at the latest, rescheduled, postponed.

title: Listen to an Academic Talk
lines: The academic talk is the longest listening task: a professor or lecturer speaks for about one to two minutes (160-250 words) on a topic from science, social science, the humanities or business. Four questions follow. It is the task most like real university study, and it rewards good note-taking and an understanding of how lectures are organized.
## What is on the screen
- While you listen, you may see a picture of the speaker or a classroom, and sometimes a key term on a board.
- You hear the talk once only. Notes are allowed.
- After the talk, four multiple-choice questions appear, with four options each.
## Timing
Listening takes about 29 minutes in all, in two adaptive stages. Academic talks appear mainly in the harder parts. Expect about 1.5 to 2 minutes of listening, then roughly 30 seconds per question.
## What is being tested
- The main idea: what the talk is mainly about.
- Key details: definitions, causes, results, steps.
- The purpose of an example: why the speaker mentions a story, an animal, a company or a historical case.
- Organization: how the talk is built (definition then examples, problem then solution, a comparison, a sequence).
- Attitude: whether the speaker is sure, doubtful, critical or enthusiastic.
- Inference: what the speaker suggests but does not say directly.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: The first 20 seconds usually give the topic and the speaker's plan: "Today we'll look at ...", "There are two main explanations for ...". Write the topic at the top of your notes.
- Step 2: Note the structure with short labels: DEF for definition, EX for example, 1 and 2 for points, vs for a contrast, -> for cause and effect.
- Step 3: When you hear an example, write it next to the point it supports. Purpose-of-example questions ask about this link, not about the example itself.
- Step 4: Listen for the speaker's opinion: "I find this convincing", "That's a bit of a stretch", "Many people assume ... but". Note it with a plus or a minus.
- Step 5: Listen for emphasis and repetition. Speakers repeat or stress what is important: "The key point here is ...", "Remember that ...".
- Step 6: When answering, use the plan you noted. The main-idea option should cover the whole talk, not one example.
## Signal language in lectures
- Topic and plan: today, let's turn to, I want to focus on, there are a few reasons.
- Definition: what we call, this is known as, in other words, basically.
- Example: for instance, take, consider, a good example is, imagine.
- Contrast: however, on the other hand, but, whereas, unlike.
- Cause and result: because of this, as a result, this leads to, that's why.
- Attitude: surprisingly, unfortunately, the problem with that is, I'd argue.
## Worked example 1

> You hear (a psychology lecture): Let's talk about something called the spacing effect. Basically, people remember information better when they study it in several short sessions spread over time, rather than in one long session. Most students know the opposite habit: studying everything the night before the exam. That can work for the next morning, but much of the material is forgotten within days. Why does spacing help? One explanation is that each time you return to the material, you have to work a little to recall it, and that effort makes the memory stronger. Think about learning to drive. Nobody learns by driving for ten hours on one day. Short, regular lessons build a skill that lasts. So for your own revision, a plan with short sessions over two weeks will usually beat one long night.
> Question 1: What is the talk mainly about?
> A. Why students should learn to drive
> B. A study method based on how memory works
> C. The dangers of studying late at night
> D. How long exams should be
B covers the definition, the explanation and the advice. A is the example, not the topic. C is a narrow and slightly distorted detail.
> Question 2: Why does the professor mention learning to drive?
> A. To show that driving is harder than studying
> B. To compare a familiar skill with the spacing effect
> C. To suggest that students should take driving lessons
> D. To explain why people forget information
B: the driving example illustrates short, regular practice. This is the most common pattern: the example supports the main concept.
> Question 3: What can be inferred about studying the night before an exam?
> A. It never helps at all.
> B. It may help in the short term but not for long-term memory.
> C. It is better than spacing for difficult subjects.
> D. Most professors recommend it.
B: "That can work for the next morning, but much of the material is forgotten within days." A is too extreme; C and D are not stated.
## Worked example 2

> You hear (a geology lecture): Some of you might think of sand dunes as something that sits still, like a hill. But dunes move. Wind pushes sand grains up the gentle side of the dune, facing the wind. At the top, the grains fall down the steep side, the one away from the wind. Grain by grain, the whole dune shifts forward. In some deserts, dunes travel several meters a year, and that can be a real problem for roads and farms. One solution that has been used is planting rows of grasses and shrubs, because their roots hold the sand in place. It's not a perfect fix, but in many places it has slowed the dunes considerably.
> Question: How is the talk organized?
> A. A common belief is corrected, a process is explained, and then a problem and a solution are discussed.
> B. Two types of dune are compared.
> C. Several theories about deserts are presented and rejected.
> D. The history of desert research is described in time order.
A. "Some of you might think ... But dunes move" corrects a belief, the wind and grains describe a process, and roads and plants give a problem and a solution.
> Question: What is the professor's attitude toward planting grasses and shrubs?
> A. She thinks it solves the problem completely.
> B. She believes it is useful but limited.
> C. She doubts that it has any effect.
> D. She thinks it damages farms.
B, from "It's not a perfect fix, but ... it has slowed the dunes considerably." A and C are the two extremes the tone rules out.
! For attitude questions, the answer is often in a short phrase with a hedge: not a perfect fix, a bit of a stretch, fairly convincing. Write these down with a plus or minus sign.
## Common traps
- Choosing the example as the main idea.
- Options that state a detail correctly but give the wrong reason for it.
- Extreme options about attitude when the speaker hedges.
- Confusing the steps of a process or which side of a contrast a detail belongs to.
- Options that sound like general knowledge but were not said.
## How to practise between mocks
- Listen to short academic videos and open university lectures for 5-10 minutes a day. Take notes, then write a three-line summary: topic, main points, one example and its purpose.
- Build a personal set of note symbols and use it every time.
- Learn the signal language above and listen for it actively.
- Study academic vocabulary with this app's flashcards; many lecture words (hypothesis, evidence, factor, process) appear across subjects.
- Practise once-only listening: no pausing during the talk, then check the script after answering.

title: Listen and Choose a Response
lines: Listen and Choose a Response is the task you will see most often in Listening. One person says a short line, such as a question, a request, an offer, a complaint or a piece of news, and you choose the most natural reply from four written options. It tests whether you understand what the speaker really means and how people actually answer in conversation.
## What is on the screen
- You hear one line of 4-20 words, once. The line is not shown in writing.
- Four written replies appear. You choose one.
- There is a short time to answer, then the next line plays. The items come quickly one after another.
## Timing

Listening takes about 29 minutes in all, in two adaptive stages. This task appears in both stages, so it carries many points. You have only a few seconds per item, so you must decide fast; there is no time to replay or think for long.
## What is being tested
- The function of the line: is it a question, an invitation, a request, a suggestion, a complaint, an apology or news?
- Indirect answers: real people often answer a yes/no question without saying yes or no.
- Idioms and everyday expressions: "I'm swamped", "it's on me", "count me in", "that rings a bell".
- Grammar of replies: tense, person and question type must match the line.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: While listening, catch the first words. "Where", "When", "Would you mind", "Why don't we", "Did you" tell you what kind of reply is needed.
- Step 2: Decide the function in your head in one word: offer, request, news, complaint.
- Step 3: Read the four replies quickly and cross out the ones that answer a different question or use the wrong tense or person.
- Step 4: Of the remaining replies, choose the one a polite, real person would say. It is often indirect.
- Step 5: Do not dwell on a missed item. Guess and get ready for the next line.
## Common indirect-reply patterns
- Giving a reason instead of no. "Want to get coffee after class?" "I've got a lab until four." (This means no, or not now.)
- Giving a condition. "Can you help me move on Saturday?" "Sure, as long as it's after lunch."
- Answering with the information behind the question. "Is the library still open?" "It closes at ten on weekdays."
- Passing the question to someone else. "Who's leading the seminar tomorrow?" "Check the course page; they posted it there."
- Answering a question with a question. "Should we take the bus or walk?" "How much time do we have?"
- Suggesting an alternative. "The printer in the lab isn't working." "There's another one on the second floor."
- Agreeing or disagreeing with an opinion indirectly. "That lecture was really long." "I almost fell asleep." (agreement)
- Accepting an offer. "I can lend you my notes." "That would be a huge help."
- Responding to news with an emotion or a follow-up. "I got the internship!" "Congratulations! When do you start?"
- Responding to an apology. "Sorry I'm late." "No problem, we just started."
- Responding to a tag question. "The deadline is Friday, isn't it?" "Actually, they moved it to Monday."
## Worked example 1
> You hear: Do you know if the bookstore takes returns on used textbooks?
> A. Yes, I bought my textbooks last week.
> B. Only within two weeks, and you'll need the receipt.
> C. I'll return it to you tomorrow.
> D. It's the book with the red cover.

B answers the real question (the return policy) with a condition. A answers a different question (did you buy books?), and it only repeats "textbooks". C uses "return" with a different meaning (giving something back to a person). D describes a book, which no one asked about.
## Worked example 2
> You hear: I was wondering if you could cover my shift at the help desk on Thursday.
> A. I covered the table with a cloth.
> B. The help desk is next to the main entrance.
> C. I've got an exam that afternoon, but I'm free in the morning.
> D. Thursday was a busy day for me.

C is a natural indirect reply: a reason plus a partial offer. A is a sound and word trap: "cover" with its physical meaning. B gives a location that was not asked. D uses the wrong tense; the request is about the coming Thursday, not a past one.
## Worked example 3 (harder)
> You hear: You haven't seen my blue folder anywhere, have you?
> A. No, I haven't been to the folder.
> B. Did you check under the papers on your desk?
> C. Yes, I have seen it many blue times.
> D. I'd rather have a green one.
B is the natural reply: a helpful question instead of a plain yes or no. A and C are grammatically or socially odd. D answers as if the line were an offer to choose a color.
! A reply that repeats a word you heard, or a word that sounds like it, is often a trap. Real replies usually use new words.
## Common traps
- Same word, different meaning: "cover", "return", "check", "run", "break".
- Similar sounds: "walk" and "work", "lend" and "land", "fourteen" and "forty".
- Wrong tense or person: answering a future plan in the past, or answering "Did you ...?" with "Yes, he did."
- A reply to a different question type: answering "where" with a time, or answering "why" with "yes".
- Socially odd replies: too rude, too formal, or ignoring the feeling in the speaker's voice.
- Choosing the only reply that says yes or no directly, when the indirect one is more natural.
## How to practise between mocks
- Listen to short dialogs in English (podcasts for learners, TV comedies, campus videos) and pause after each line: predict a natural reply before you hear it.
- Learn common idioms and conversational expressions in groups: agreeing, refusing politely, offering, accepting, showing surprise.
- Practise question forms: tag questions, negative questions ("Didn't you ...?") and indirect questions ("Do you know if ...?").
- Train speed: do 10 items in a row without pausing, then review every mistake and name the trap.
- Say replies aloud. Producing natural answers makes it easier to recognize them.

title: Listen to a Conversation
lines: In this task you hear a short conversation between two people, usually students, a student and a staff member, or friends in an everyday setting. Each conversation is about 80-150 words long with 6-10 turns, and it is followed by two questions.
## What is on the screen
- While you listen, the screen may show a simple picture of the setting or the speakers. The questions do not appear until the conversation ends.
- After the audio, two multiple-choice questions appear, one at a time, with four options each.
- You hear the conversation once only. You may take notes.
## Timing

Listening lasts about 29 minutes in total, in two adaptive stages. A conversation takes under a minute to hear; then you have a short time for each question. Keep moving: you cannot go back to earlier questions after the next recording starts.
## What is being tested
- The gist: why the people are talking and what the main topic is.
- Key details: a time, a reason, a change of plan, a problem.
- A speaker's purpose or attitude: is she pleased, worried, unsure, surprised?
- What will happen next: the final decision or plan.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: The first two turns usually show the reason for the conversation. Listen hard at the start: "I'm here because ...", "Do you have a minute? I wanted to ask about ...".
- Step 2: Take short notes in two columns, one for each speaker. Write key words only: problem, reason, suggestion, decision.
- Step 3: Listen for changes in direction: "Actually ...", "Oh, but ...", "The thing is ...", "In that case ...". The answer often comes right after such words.
- Step 4: Listen for tone. "Oh, great" can be real pleasure or disappointment, depending on the voice and the context.
- Step 5: The last turns usually give the plan. Questions about what will happen next are answered there.
- Step 6: When the questions come, answer the gist question from your overall understanding, and detail questions from your notes.
## Worked example 1
> Woman (student): Hi, I'm trying to register for the advanced photography class, but the system says it's full.
> Man (office assistant): Let me see. Yes, all twenty places are taken. There is a waiting list, though.
> Woman: How long is it?
> Man: Only three names right now. People often drop the class in the first week, so you have a good chance.
> Woman: Okay. I'd rather not wait without a backup, though. Is there anything similar?
> Man: There's a digital imaging course on Tuesday evenings. It covers editing more than shooting.
> Woman: That might work. Can I join the waiting list and register for the evening course too?
> Man: Sure, and if a photography place opens, you can switch.
> Question 1: Why does the woman go to the office?
> A. To complain about the photography teacher
> B. To get help with a class that has no places left
> C. To drop the digital imaging course
> D. To buy equipment for a photography class
B, from her first turn. The answer paraphrases "the system says it's full" as "no places left". D and A are not mentioned; C reverses her plan.
> Question 2: What will the woman probably do?
> A. Wait for the first week of classes before deciding
> B. Take only the digital imaging course
> C. Join the waiting list and sign up for a second course
> D. Ask the teacher to add a twenty-first place
C repeats her final plan in new words. A is what she says she would rather not do. B ignores the waiting list.
## Worked example 2
> Man: Amara, did you finish the slides for our presentation?
> Woman: Most of them. I'm stuck on the chart for the survey results.
> Man: Oh, I can do that part. I made one for my economics class last week.
> Woman: Really? That would save me hours. But you're already writing the conclusion.
> Man: The conclusion's almost done. Send me the numbers tonight.
> Woman: You're a lifesaver. I'll email them as soon as I get home.
> Question: What does the woman mean when she says "You're a lifesaver"?
> A. She thinks the man works in a hospital.
> B. She is very grateful for his help.
> C. She is worried about his safety.
> D. She wants him to give the presentation.
B. "Lifesaver" is an idiom for someone who helps at an important moment. A and C take the words literally.
## What good notes look like
For worked example 1, useful notes take ten seconds to write and are enough to answer both questions:
> W: photo class full
> M: wait list, 3 names, drop wk 1
> W: backup? -> digital imaging, Tue eve
> PLAN: wait list + eve course, switch later
Notice that the notes capture the problem, the suggestions and the final plan, not every word.
## Common traps
- Options that repeat words from the conversation but change who did what.
- A suggestion that was made and rejected, presented as the final decision.
- Details that are true but do not answer the gist question.
- Literal readings of idioms ("lifesaver", "on the same page", "running behind").
- Missing the change of plan that comes after "actually" or "but".
! Many next-action questions are answered in the last two turns. Keep your attention until the very end of the recording.
## How to practise between mocks
- Listen to everyday conversations in English: campus videos, learner podcasts, TV series about students or offices. After each scene, say who talked, why, and what they decided.
- Practise note-taking with symbols: arrows for change, a check for agreement, a question mark for uncertainty.
- Learn common conversational idioms and phrases for suggestions, agreement and refusal.
- Practise listening once only. Do not pause or replay in practice sets; review the script only after you answer.

title: Listen and Repeat
lines: Listen and Repeat starts the Speaking section. You are placed in a scenario, for example training as a guide at a science museum or starting a job at a campus cafe. A speaker says seven sentences, one at a time, and you repeat each one exactly. The sentences start short and become longer and more complex, up to about 20 words.
## What is on the screen
- A short description of the scenario and a picture of the place.
- For each sentence: you hear it once, then a short recording time begins and you repeat it aloud. The sentence is not shown in writing.
- Seven sentences in a row, with no preparation time. In this app's mock you have about 12 seconds to repeat each one.
## Scoring

The Speaking section takes about 8 minutes in all. Your repetitions are scored on how completely and accurately you repeat the words and on how clear your speech is: pronunciation, stress and rhythm. Each task is scored on a 0-5 scale. Missing words, changing words or long pauses lower the score; a small accent does not, as long as you are easy to understand.
## What is being tested
- Listening accuracy: catching every word, including small ones (a, the, to, has, were).
- Short-term memory for language: holding a whole sentence for a few seconds.
- Grammar knowledge: you remember sentences better when you understand their structure.
- Pronunciation: word stress, sentence rhythm, linking and clear endings (-s, -ed).
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Read the scenario. It tells you the kind of vocabulary you will hear (a museum, a lab, a hotel, a store).
- Step 2: While listening, do not try to remember sounds; follow the meaning. Picture the instruction: "Visitors should leave their bags in the lockers near the main entrance."
- Step 3: Chunk the sentence into meaning groups: Visitors should leave their bags / in the lockers / near the main entrance.
- Step 4: Start repeating as soon as the recording time begins. Speak at a natural, steady pace; do not rush and do not speak word by word.
- Step 5: Copy the speaker's stress and intonation, like an echo. Stress the content words (visitors, leave, bags, lockers, main, entrance).
- Step 6: If you forget part of a sentence, keep going with the rest. A complete sentence with one small change scores better than stopping.
## How the sentences grow
In a typical set, sentences move through patterns like these:
- Short imperatives and statements: "Please wear your badge."
- Sentences with a place or time phrase: "The tour starts at ten in the main hall."
- Two clauses joined by and, but, because or so.
- Time and condition clauses: "If a visitor asks for directions, show them the map at the front desk."
- Relative clauses and passives: "The paintings that were moved last week are now displayed on the second floor."
- Numbers, names of rooms and days, and lists: "Groups of more than fifteen people need to book at least two days in advance."
## Worked example 1 (scenario: assistant at a university library)
> 1. Check the return cart every hour.
> Chunks: Check the return cart / every hour. Stress: CHECK, reTURN CART, EVery HOUR.
> 2. Students who need a quiet room can book one online.
> Chunks: Students who need a quiet room / can book one / online. The relative clause "who need a quiet room" belongs to "Students"; keep it in one breath.
> 3. If the printer runs out of paper, you'll find more in the cabinet behind the front desk.
> Chunks: If the printer runs out of paper, / you'll find more / in the cabinet / behind the front desk. Two common errors: dropping the -s in "runs" and saying "you find" instead of "you'll find".
## Worked example 2 (scenario: volunteer at a city botanical garden)
> 4. The greenhouse closes thirty minutes earlier than the rest of the garden on weekdays.
> Chunks: The greenhouse closes / thirty minutes earlier / than the rest of the garden / on weekdays. Say "thirty" clearly so it is not heard as "thirteen": stress the first syllable, THIR-ty.
> 5. Visitors are asked not to touch the plants that have been labeled with a red sign.

> Chunks: Visitors are asked / not to touch the plants / that have been labeled / with a red sign. Keep the passive "are asked" and "have been labeled"; learners often simplify them to "ask" and "labeled".
! When you understand the grammar of a sentence, you can rebuild small words from it. If you remember "have been labeled", the "have" and "been" come back automatically.
## Common traps
- Replacing words with synonyms ("big" for "large", "start" for "begin"). The task asks for the exact words.
- Dropping small words: articles, auxiliaries, prepositions.
- Losing endings: -s on verbs and plurals, -ed on past forms.
- Waiting too long before starting, so the sentence fades from memory.
- Speaking too fast and unclearly to "get everything in", or too slowly, word by word.
- Stopping completely after a mistake.
## How to practise between mocks
- Shadowing: play a short clip of natural English (a podcast, a news report, an audio guide) and speak along with it, a fraction of a second behind the speaker.
- Repeat-after-pause: pause after each sentence and repeat it exactly, then check with the transcript.
- Record yourself and compare with the original: which words did you change or miss?
- Practise sentences with numbers, room names and times; these are easy to mix up.
- Learn the rhythm of English: content words stressed, function words reduced ("to" sounds like "tuh", "and" like "n").
- Practise the grammar patterns above, especially relative clauses and passives, so they feel natural to say.

title: Read an Academic Passage
lines: Read an Academic Passage is the closest task to university reading. You get a passage of about 200 words from a textbook-style source on a topic such as ecology, geology, art history, psychology or business, and five questions about it. You do not need any background knowledge: everything you need is in the passage, and outside knowledge can even mislead you.
## What is on the screen
- The passage, usually one or two paragraphs. Long passages can be scrolled.
- Five multiple-choice questions, one at a time or in a list, each with four options.
- Some questions highlight a word or sentence in the passage so you can find it fast.
## Timing

The task is part of the Reading module (about 30 minutes for the whole section). Plan about 4 to 5 minutes per passage: 1.5 to 2 minutes to read, then about 30-40 seconds per question. If a question is taking too long, choose the best option and move on.
## Question types
- Main idea: What is the passage mainly about? What is the main point of the paragraph?
- Detail: According to the passage, what ...?
- Negative fact: All of the following are mentioned EXCEPT ...
- Vocabulary in context: The word "X" in the passage is closest in meaning to ...
- Reference: The word "it" or "this" in the passage refers to ...
- Inference: What can be inferred about ...?
- Purpose: Why does the author mention ...? What is the purpose of the second sentence?
- Organization: How is the information in the passage organized?
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Read the first sentence and the last sentence of the passage first. Together they usually show the topic and the main point.

- Step 2: Read the whole passage once, building a quick mental map: claim, explanation, example, contrast, conclusion. Notice signal words: however, for example, as a result, in contrast, in addition, this suggests.
- Step 3: Answer the main idea question with the map, not with one sentence. The correct answer covers the whole passage.
- Step 4: For detail, negative fact and reference questions, go back to the exact place. For reference questions, put each option in place of the pronoun and check the sentence still makes sense.
- Step 5: For vocabulary questions, use the sentence, not your memory. Substitute each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning.
- Step 6: For purpose questions, ask what job the sentence or example does: support a claim, give a contrast, define a term, show an exception.
- Step 7: For inference, choose what the passage strongly supports. Reject options that go further than the text.
## Worked example 1

> Many desert plants survive long dry periods by storing water in thick stems or leaves. Cacti are the best-known example: their stems can swell after rain and shrink slowly as the water is used. Other species take a different approach. Instead of storing water, they avoid drought altogether by completing their life cycle quickly. After a rare heavy rain, their seeds germinate, the plants flower and produce new seeds within a few weeks, and then the adults die. The seeds may then wait in the soil for years until the next good rain. A third group relies on very deep roots that reach water far below the surface. These strategies show that there is no single solution to life in a dry climate.
> Question: What is the passage mainly about?
> A. Why cacti are the most successful desert plants
> B. Different ways in which plants deal with a lack of water
> C. How desert seeds can survive for many years
> D. The effect of heavy rain on desert soil

B matches the map: storing water, avoiding drought, deep roots, and the conclusion "no single solution". A is too narrow and too extreme ("most successful" is not stated). C is one detail. D is not discussed.
> Question: Why does the author mention cacti?
> A. To give a familiar example of the first strategy
> B. To argue that storing water is the best strategy
> C. To contrast them with plants that have deep roots
> D. To explain why some seeds wait for years
A: the passage says cacti are "the best-known example" of storing water. Purpose questions ask about the job of the detail; here the job is illustration.
> Question: What can be inferred about the plants that complete their life cycle quickly?
> A. They grow larger than cacti.
> B. Their adult plants are rarely seen during dry years.
> C. They need deep roots to survive.
> D. They store water in their seeds.

B follows from the text: the adults die after a few weeks, and the seeds wait until the next good rain, so in dry years there are few or no adult plants. A and D are not supported; C belongs to the third group.
## Worked example 2

> Visitors who see ancient Egyptian wall paintings for the first time often think the artists lacked skill, because the figures look flat and stiff. Historians of art see it differently. Egyptian painters were usually not trying to copy what the eye sees from one position. A person was often shown with the face in profile but the eye and shoulders from the front, so that each part appeared in its clearest, most recognizable view. Size followed the same logic: an important official might be painted much larger than the servants around him to show his rank, not his height. From this point of view, the apparent "errors" were deliberate choices that served the purpose of the image.
> Question: The word "deliberate" in the passage is closest in meaning to
> A. careless
> B. intentional
> C. expensive
> D. traditional

B. The contrast between apparent "errors" and "choices that served the purpose" shows that the painters meant to paint this way. A is the opposite. D might seem reasonable, but it does not fit the idea of choice.
> Question: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
> A. A process is described in the order in which it happens.
> B. A common first impression is presented and then challenged with examples.
> C. Two styles of painting are compared and one is judged better.
> D. A problem is described and several solutions are proposed.

B: the first sentence gives the visitors' impression, "Historians of art see it differently" challenges it, and the examples of the profile view and of size support the new view. D is tempting because "errors" sounds like a problem, but no solutions are proposed.
! In organization questions, look for turning-point words such as "However", "see it differently" or "In contrast". They divide the passage into its parts.
## Common traps
- Options that copy long phrases from the passage but change one key relationship (cause becomes effect, before becomes after, some becomes all).
- Too narrow main-idea options that describe only one example.
- Too extreme options with best, always, never, only, completely.
- Outside knowledge: an option that is true in real life but not stated in the passage.
- In EXCEPT questions, forgetting to find the one option that is NOT mentioned. Check each option against the text and cross out the three that are there.
- Reference errors: a pronoun usually refers to the nearest noun that makes sense in number and meaning, not always the nearest noun.
## How to practise between mocks

- Read one short academic text every day: textbook introductions, encyclopedia articles, science magazine pieces. After reading, write the main idea in one sentence and list the parts (claim, example, contrast).
- Build academic vocabulary with the flashcards in this app, especially words with several meanings and their synonyms.
- Practise signal words: make a list grouped by function (contrast, addition, cause, result, example) and notice them as you read.

- After each practice set, classify every mistake by question type. If most mistakes are inference or purpose questions, practise asking "what job does this sentence do?" for every sentence in a paragraph.
- Do not reread the whole passage for every question; train yourself to go straight to the right place using your mental map.

title: Read in Daily Life: short texts
lines: Read in Daily Life uses the kind of English you will meet every day as a student abroad: notices on a door, a text from a classmate, a cafe menu, a bus timetable, a post in a campus group. The short version of the task gives you a text of about 25-80 words and two questions about it.
## What is on the screen
- The text appears on the left or top of the screen, often laid out like the real thing: a sign, a phone message, a small table or a social media post.
- Two multiple-choice questions follow, each with four options and one correct answer.

- Typical questions: What is the purpose of the notice? According to the message, what time does the event start? What does the phrase "on the house" mean? What should readers do if they want a refund?
## Timing

There is no separate timer for this task; it is part of the Reading module (about 30 minutes for all of Reading). Short texts should be quick points: aim for about 1 minute per text, including both questions. Time saved here is time you can spend on the academic passage.
## What is being tested
- Understanding the purpose of a practical text: to inform, to warn, to invite, to request, to advertise, to apologize.
- Finding a key detail quickly (a date, a price, a condition, a place).
- Understanding everyday phrases and abbreviations in context: "sold out", "while supplies last", "ASAP", "RSVP", "no later than".
- Working out what the reader is expected to do.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Look at the shape of the text first. Is it a sign, a message, a menu? Who wrote it and for whom? This takes two seconds and tells you the likely purpose.
- Step 2: Read the whole text once. It is short; reading the questions first saves very little here.
- Step 3: Read the first question and predict the answer before looking at the options.
- Step 4: Choose the option that matches your prediction in meaning, not in words. Correct answers usually paraphrase ("closed for repairs" becomes "temporarily unavailable").
- Step 5: For detail questions, go back and find the exact line. Check conditions such as "only", "except", "after", "before" and "unless".
- Step 6: For purpose questions, ask what the writer wants to happen. A notice that mentions a change in hours exists to inform people of the change, not to describe the building.
## Worked example 1
> Text message from Kwame: Hey, the study group is moving to Room 214 tonight, our usual room is booked for an exam. Same time, 7:00. Can you bring the extension cord? Mine is broken.
> Question: Why did Kwame send the message?
> A. To cancel tonight's study group
> B. To tell a friend about a change of location
> C. To ask a friend to repair an extension cord
> D. To invite a friend to take an exam

Predict first: the main news is the new room. B paraphrases "moving to Room 214". A is wrong because the meeting still happens ("same time"). C mixes two details: he asks his friend to bring a cord, and it is his own cord that is broken. D takes the word "exam" from the reason and builds a false idea around it.
> Question: What does Kwame ask his friend to do?
> A. Book a different room
> B. Arrive earlier than usual
> C. Bring an item to the meeting
> D. Lend him money for a new cord
C paraphrases "bring the extension cord" with a general word, "an item". B contradicts "same time", and A and D are not mentioned.
## Worked example 2
> Sign at a campus cafe: Hot breakfast served 7:30-10:30 a.m. weekdays only. After 10:30, sandwiches and salads are available until closing. Reusable cup? Take 25 cents off any drink.
> Question: What can be inferred about the cafe on Saturdays?
> A. It does not serve hot breakfast.
> B. It closes at 10:30 a.m.
> C. Drinks are cheaper than on weekdays.
> D. Only sandwiches are sold.

A is correct because hot breakfast is "weekdays only", and Saturday is not a weekday. B confuses the end of breakfast with closing time. C twists the cup discount, which has nothing to do with the day. D is too extreme: the sign says nothing about which other food is sold on Saturdays.
## Common traps
- Word-match options: an option that repeats a striking word from the text ("exam", "broken") but changes the meaning.
- Mixing two details: the right people, the wrong action; the right time, the wrong day.
- Too extreme: "always", "never", "only", "all" when the text is less absolute.
- True but not the answer: a fact from the text that does not answer this question.
- Missing small words that change the meaning: "no later than Friday" means Friday or earlier; "except Sundays" removes a day.
! In purpose questions, the first line often states the news and the rest gives details. Do not choose a detail as the purpose.
## Everyday language to know
- Notices: until further notice, closed for maintenance, out of order, staff only, by appointment only.
- Shopping and food: on sale, sold out, while supplies last, complimentary, on the house, gluten-free, take-out.
- Messages: running late, heads up, can you cover for me, let me know, no worries, ASAP.
- Deadlines: due by, no later than, at the latest, extended to, postponed until.
## How to practise between mocks
- Read real everyday English: shop signs in English, bus and train timetables, product labels, university web pages and student union notices.
- For every text you read, say in one sentence who wrote it, why, and what the reader should do.
- Collect phrases that have a special meaning in notices (such as "until further notice") in a notebook with an example.
- In practice sets, write down why each wrong option is wrong; you will start to see the same four or five trap types again and again.
- Work on speed: time yourself on sets of short texts and try to keep to about one minute each without losing accuracy.

title: Read in Daily Life: longer texts
lines: The longer version of Read in Daily Life gives you a practical text of about 90-160 words with three questions. The texts are the ones a student deals with every week: an email from a landlord, a campus announcement, a flyer for a workshop, instructions for a new device, a web page about library services, or a short thread of messages between two people.
## What is on the screen
- One text, laid out to look like its real form: an email with a subject line, a poster with headings, a web page with sections, or a message thread with names and times.
- Three multiple-choice questions, four options each.
- Question types: the purpose of the text, a detail, an inference, the meaning of a word or phrase in context, and what someone will probably do next.
## Timing
This task is part of the Reading module (about 30 minutes for all of Reading, in two stages). Aim for about 2 to 2.5 minutes per text: around 50 seconds to read, then about 30 seconds per question.
## What is being tested
- Following the organization of a practical text: headings, steps, conditions and exceptions.
- Locating information quickly and reading it exactly.
- Making a small inference: what is implied but not stated.
- Understanding a word's meaning in this context, which may differ from its most common meaning.
- Understanding a sequence of messages: who asked, who answered, and what was agreed.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Use the layout. Read the subject line, title or headings first. In a thread, note who is writing and in what order.
- Step 2: Read the text once at a steady pace. Notice the purpose (often stated in the first two lines) and any change, request, condition or deadline.
- Step 3: Read each question and decide its type. Purpose and inference questions need the whole text; detail and vocabulary questions need one line.
- Step 4: For detail questions, find the exact place and compare carefully. For vocabulary questions, replace the word with each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning of the sentence.
- Step 5: For inference questions, choose the option that must be true from the text, not one that might be true.
- Step 6: For next-action questions, look at the end of the text: the last request, the next step or the agreement in a thread.
## Worked example 1
> Subject: Laundry room update
> Dear residents of Maple Hall,

> The two washing machines on the ground floor will be replaced next week. Work begins Monday morning and should be finished by Wednesday evening. During this time, please use the laundry room in Birch Hall, which is open 24 hours with your student card. The new machines will accept payment by card or through the campus app, so you will no longer need coins. If you still have credit on an old laundry card, bring it to the front desk before the end of the month to have the balance moved to your student account.
> Thank you for your patience,
> Sofia Reyes, Residence Office
> Question 1: What is the main purpose of the email?
> A. To explain how to use the campus app
> B. To inform residents about a temporary change and new equipment
> C. To ask residents to clean the laundry room
> D. To announce that Birch Hall will close next week

B covers the whole email: machines are out for a few days, there is a place to go meanwhile, and new machines are coming. A is a minor detail. C is not mentioned. D reverses the information: Birch Hall is the alternative and stays open.
> Question 2: The word "balance" in the email is closest in meaning to
> A. stability
> B. comparison
> C. remaining money
> D. payment method

In "have the balance moved to your student account", balance means the money left on the card, so C. A is the most common meaning of "balance" (keeping steady), which is a typical trap in vocabulary questions.
> Question 3: What should a resident with an old laundry card probably do?
> A. Throw the card away after Wednesday
> B. Use it in the Birch Hall machines
> C. Take it to the front desk soon
> D. Add coins to it at the new machines

C follows from the last instruction: bring it to the front desk before the end of the month. A ignores the money still on the card; B and D are not supported, and D also contradicts "no longer need coins".
## Worked example 2: a message thread
In a thread, track the conversation like a story: who asks, who offers, and what is finally agreed.
> Chen (9:02): Does anyone have a calculator I could borrow for Thursday's statistics exam? Mine stopped working.
> Amara (9:10): I have one, but I need it for my own exam on Thursday morning. It finishes at noon.
> Chen (9:12): That's perfect, mine isn't until 3. Could I pick it up from you at lunch?
> Amara (9:15): Sure. I'll be in the cafeteria by 12:30.
> Question: What will Amara probably do on Thursday?
> A. Take Chen's statistics exam with him
> B. Use the calculator and then give it to Chen
> C. Buy Chen a new calculator at lunch
> D. Lend the calculator to Chen before 9:00

B combines the final agreement: she uses it in the morning and hands it over at lunch. D gets the order wrong, and A and C invent actions. Wrong options in threads often give the right object to the wrong person or at the wrong time.
## Common traps
- The most common meaning of a word, when the context needs a less common one (balance, issue, figure, cover, note, run).
- An option that is true according to one line but not the main purpose.
- Possible but not stated: inference answers must be supported by the text.
- Reversed roles in threads: who asked and who offered.
- Conditions and exceptions: "students who registered before May 1", "except holidays", "unless it rains".
! Before you choose an inference answer, point to the line that supports it. If you cannot point, it is probably a trap.
## How to practise between mocks
- Read university web pages in English: housing, library, IT help, student services. They are exactly this style.
- Practise vocabulary in context: write down common words with a second meaning (a "figure" in a report, to "run" a club, to "cover" a shift).
- After reading an email or notice, summarize it in one sentence of your own words; this trains purpose questions.
- Time yourself: three questions in about two and a half minutes, then review each wrong option and name its trap type.
